summary: The Chandelas of Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand) rose from vassals of the Gurjara-Pratiharas to sovereign kings under Dhanga in the later 10th century, ruling from Khajuraho, the fortress of Kalanjara and later Mahoba. Vidyadhara stood up to Mahmud of Ghazni in 1019 and 1022, but Kalachuri attacks, the sack of Mahoba by Prithviraj Chauhan in c. 1182–83 and the Delhi Sultanate's capture of Kalanjara in 1202–03 wore the kingdom down. Trailokyavarman won back much of the old domain, yet by the time of Hammiravarman (c. 1288–1311) the kings had dropped their imperial titles, and the main line ended around 1315.
details: The Chandelas began in the 9th century as a small kingdom around Khajuraho, ruling as vassals of the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj. As Pratihara power weakened, Yashovarman (c. 925–950) became practically independent, captured the great fort of Kalanjara and commissioned the Lakshmana Temple at Khajuraho. His son Dhanga, who reigned from about 950 to 999, went further. His inscriptions no longer name a Pratihara overlord, which historians read as a formal claim to sovereignty. The Chandelas now ruled the Vindhyan country of Bundelkhand in their own right and became one of the leading powers of northern India.

Dhanga's reign of almost half a century was remembered as a high point of Chandela power. Court inscriptions boast of conquests far to the east and south, and claim that the rulers of Kosala and other lands obeyed the commands of his officers, though historians treat such claims as poetic exaggeration. At Khajuraho he built the Vishvanatha Temple, dedicated to Shiva, one of the finest of the town's sandstone temples. Dhanga died around 999. His son Ganda held the kingdom together for a few years before Vidyadhara, the most powerful of the Chandela kings, succeeded him.

In about 1018 Mahmud of Ghazni marched deep into northern India and sacked Kannauj, the old Pratihara capital, after its king, possibly Rajyapala, fled. The Arab historian Ibn al-Athir says that 'Bida', king of Khajuraho, a form of Vidyadhara's name, then killed the Kannauj king as punishment for his cowardice. An inscription at Dubkund credits the deed to Arjuna of the Kachchhapaghata family, who probably acted for Vidyadhara as his ally or vassal. The episode showed that the Chandelas, not the fading Pratiharas, now led the defence of the Ganges plain, and it set Vidyadhara on a collision course with Mahmud.

Mahmud returned in 1019 to punish Vidyadhara. On the way he defeated the Kabul Shahi ruler Trilochanapala and sacked Bari, the new Pratihara capital, before meeting the Chandela army. The chroniclers disagree about what followed. Nizamuddin Ahmad says there was no battle: Vidyadhara slipped away at night, leaving his camp to be plundered, including 580 elephants. Ibn al-Athir instead describes a battle that ended at nightfall. Either way the Chandela kingdom survived intact, and Mahmud went home with booty rather than new territory.

In 1022 Mahmud invaded again. He first besieged Gwalior, held by Vidyadhara's Kachchhapaghata vassal Kirtiraja, and lifted the siege after four days for 35 elephants. He then laid a long siege to Kalanjara, the Chandela stronghold. According to the Muslim chronicles, Vidyadhara offered 300 elephants and asked for safety, and Firishta adds that Mahmud gave him fifteen fortresses in return. The historian S. K. Mitra reads the deal as an exchange of gifts. Vidyadhara, who also commissioned the Kandariya Mahadeva Temple at Khajuraho, kept a kingdom stretching from the Chambal to the Narmada.

By the end of Vidyadhara's reign the Ghaznavid wars had weakened the kingdom. Its southern neighbours, the Kalachuris of Tripuri near modern Jabalpur, took advantage. Their king Gangeya-deva conquered the eastern parts of the Chandela lands, although Vidyadhara's successor Vijayapala is said to have beaten him in battle. Gangeya's son Lakshmi-Karna went further and subjugated Vijayapala's son Devavarman, who reigned c. 1050–1060. For a time the Chandelas lived in the shadow of the Kalachuris, and their power shrank back towards the core of Bundelkhand.

Devavarman's brother Kirttivarman, who reigned c. 1060–1100, restored Chandela fortunes. A Mahoba inscription says he crushed the 'haughty' Lakshmi-Karna, and the historian S. K. Mitra dates the decisive battle to around 1070. The Sanskrit play Prabodha-chandrodaya, staged at his court, credits the victory to a man named Gopala, perhaps a general or feudatory. Kirttivarman's gold coins may commemorate the triumph. A Persian poet records that Ibrahim of Ghazna attacked Kalanjara in these years, but there is no evidence that the fort was lost. The Chandelas were once more masters of Bundelkhand.

Madanavarman, who ruled c. 1128–1165, revived Chandela glory by subduing neighbouring kingdoms. An inscription of 1134 places him at Bhilsa (Vidisha), on the border with the Paramaras of Malwa, and he may have seized part of their territory, though the Paramaras won it back by about 1143–44. He may also have briefly occupied northern Baghelkhand while the Kalachuris were weak. His kingdom covered the Vindhyan lands between the Betwa and Yamuna rivers, and Mahoba, with its Madan Sagar lake and lakeside temples, flourished under him.

Paramardi (c. 1165–1203) faced the ambitious Chahamana (Chauhan) king Prithviraj III. Around 1182–83 Prithviraj invaded the Chandela kingdom and sacked Mahoba, an event confirmed by inscriptions at Madanpur. Later ballads, the source of the famous Alha-Udal legends, tell of Paramardi's generals Alha and Udal, a treacherous brother-in-law and a desperate defence, but historians doubt their details. Chandela records stay silent, probably out of shame. The blow was not fatal: Paramardi's own inscriptions from 1184 to 1201 show that he soon recovered his kingdom.

After the Ghurid conquest of northern India, their general Qutb al-Din Aibak, with Iltutmish, besieged Kalanjara in 1202 or 1203; the chronicles disagree on the year. According to Hasan Nizami, Paramardi agreed to become a vassal and pay tribute but died before paying; Firishta says a minister who opposed surrender killed him. His dewan, Aj Deo, held out until drought dried up the fort's reservoirs. Aibak appointed a governor at Kalanjara and also took Mahoba. The Chandelas had lost their two greatest strongholds, and their power never fully recovered.

Paramardi's successor Trailokyavarman (c. 1203–1245) won back much of the old domain. He took the title 'Lord of Kalanjara', suggesting that he recaptured the fortress from the Delhi Sultanate, and his coins are found across the Chandela heartland. The Persian chronicle Tabaqat-i Nasiri confirms that Kalanjara had already slipped out of Delhi's control when Iltutmish's officer Nusrat al-Din Taisi raided it in 1233. Delhi did not keep the fort, and Trailokyavarman's successors Viravarman and Bhojavarman left inscriptions at the hill fort of Ajaigarh, which became a main Chandela stronghold.

Through the 13th century the Chandelas were squeezed by the rising Muslim power of Delhi and by neighbouring dynasties. Viravarman ruled for some forty years (c. 1245–1285), followed briefly by Bhojavarman. When Hammiravarman came to the throne around 1288, he no longer used the title Maharajadhiraja, 'great king of kings', a sign of how far Chandela status had fallen. His successor Viravarman II also bore only modest titles. The main line ended around 1315, though minor branches went on ruling at Kalanjara and Mahoba; the last Kalanjara chief was killed by Sher Shah Suri's army in 1545.
